episodes.title: KISS of Light
episodes.summary: Antonija Grubisic-Cabo studies electronic band structure, the property that decides whether a material behaves as an insulator, a semiconductor or a metal. She looks at what makes materials behave the way they do electronically, and at ways to change those properties both in and out of equilibrium.
episodes.description: Antonija studies two-dimensional materials: crystals that are atomically thin and consist essentially only of surface, which makes them behave very differently from their 3D parent compounds. She uses photoemission spectroscopy to probe their electronic properties and explores how those properties shift when the substrate underneath or the surrounding environment changes, looking for new physics and future electronic devices. She arrived in the field mostly by accident, after a planned PhD in magnetism did not materialise.

episodes.title: Graphene Nanotunnels : Welcome Onboard
episodes.summary: Ashok Keerthi works on nanocarbon materials including graphene nanoribbons and two-dimensional capillaries, fabricated with atomic precision. He studies their chemical, optical, electronic and transport properties, in particular how molecules and ions move through capillaries only angstroms across.
episodes.image_alt: Ashok Keerthi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 198: Graphene Nanotunnels : Welcome Onboard — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Shattering 10,000 yr old ceramic recipe
episodes.summary: Claire Dancer looks for better ways to process ceramics and ceramic composites. More than 90 per cent of a ceramic's lifetime energy goes into making it, so cutting that is both a climate and a cost priority; the second challenge is densifying ceramics inside devices such as solid-state batteries, where the traditional high temperatures cannot be used.
episodes.image_alt: Claire Dancer on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 197: Shattering 10,000 yr old ceramic recipe — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Scaling down a chemistry lab at the Aussie Science Donut
episodes.summary: Susi Seibt points out that nanotechnology is everywhere, from smartphones to COVID rapid tests, and that much of the chemistry behind it remains a mystery because the reactions are fast and uncontrolled. She uses microfluidics, a miniature version of the flasks and tubes of a chemistry lab, together with synchrotron SAXS, to investigate those reactions on a very fast timescale.
episodes.image_alt: Susi Seibt on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 187: Scaling down a chemistry lab at the Aussie Science Donut — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Thermodynamics doesnt care about you
episodes.summary: Jose Luis Ocana Pujol studies the stability limits of scalable metamaterials, whose exotic properties come from their geometry rather than their chemistry. Because those geometric features are so small, they are slow to fabricate and prone to degrading under working conditions, which is the problem his work addresses.
episodes.image_alt: Jose Luis Ocana Pujol on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 195: Thermodynamics doesnt care about you — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Boosting green energy, one reaction at a time
episodes.summary: Rebecca Pittkowski studies new nanomaterials that can efficiently split water into hydrogen using electricity, and run the reaction in reverse inside a fuel cell. She makes these catalyst materials and uses X-rays to work out how their structure governs their efficiency.
episodes.image_alt: Rebecca Katharina Pittkowski on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 194: Boosting green energy, one reaction at a time — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanoscience from the birthplace of graphene
episodes.summary: Julien Barrier works on mesoscopic transport, the branch of physics where quantum mechanics meets the classical world: systems built from vast numbers of atoms yet small enough for quantisation effects to appear. He builds graphene electronic devices such as transistors and measures how they behave under changing temperature, magnetic field and electric bias.
episodes.image_alt: Julien Barrier on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 193: Nanoscience from the birthplace of graphene — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Harnessing Light at the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Sara Hernandez Mejias studies light conversion mechanisms where molecular biology meets spectroscopy, looking at bio-exciton coupling at the molecular level. The goal is a new class of bio-hybrid materials with light conversion customised for different applications. A physicist by training, she now leads her own group at IMDEA Nanoscience.
episodes.image_alt: Sara Hernandez Mejias on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 192: Harnessing Light at the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Everyday is a Bones Day
episodes.summary: Jessica Henty-Ridilla studies the actin and microtubule 'bones' of cells, two proteins that between them direct much of what cells normally do. Her lab focuses on what happens when that regulation goes wrong in neurodegenerative diseases such as ALS, a question she reached by way of plant biology and a postdoc on microtubules and neurons.
episodes.image_alt: Jessica Henty-Ridilla on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 191: Everyday is a Bones Day — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: To Transition or to take a Break, That's the Question
episodes.summary: Luis R. De Jesus began his chemistry degree in 2008 at the University of Puerto Rico at Cayey, a small institution within the UPR system, at a point when he was seriously considering pharmacy rather than a PhD. He works on the minute changes in bonding that occur when a solid material is put under stimulus, and has provided insight into why lithium-ion batteries fail to retain charge, charge slowly, or stop working altogether.
episodes.image_alt: Luis R. De Jesús on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 190: To Transition or to take a Break, That's the Question — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: To Transition or to take a Break, That's the Question
episodes.summary: Luis R. De Jesus studies how phase transitions occur in solids and how the electronic structure of a material changes as its bonds rearrange, with a view to using that understanding to improve how materials function.
episodes.image_alt: Luis R. De Jesús on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 189: To Transition or to take a Break, That's the Question — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Scaling down a chemistry lab at the Aussie Science Donut
episodes.summary: Susi Seibt studied polymer chemistry in a small Bavarian town and spent three months in Melbourne on a DAAD research stay during the first year of her PhD, which set the course for what followed. She regards small angle X-ray scattering as one of the most powerful characterisation techniques in materials and nanoscience; her proudest work adapted very fast nanoparticle reactions to microfluidics to watch nucleation and growth at close to nanosecond resolution.
episodes.image_alt: Susi Seibt on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 188: Scaling down a chemistry lab at the Aussie Science Donut — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Raising the stakes - nanoparticle playing cards
episodes.summary: Alexandra Brumberg did her undergraduate degree at Tufts University, starting research in her freshman year on the pleasingly esoteric problem of growing single crystals of ice. Her work, as she puts it, is all nanoscience; one graduate project took her to the National High Magnetic Field Lab in Los Alamos, New Mexico.
episodes.image_alt: Alexandra Rosen (Brumberg) on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 186: Raising the stakes - nanoparticle playing cards — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Raising the stakes - nanoparticle playing cards
episodes.summary: Alexandra Brumberg used light to study how electrons behave in nanoparticles, clusters small enough that electrons no longer behave as they do in bulk material. She now studies how nanoparticles assemble into different arrangements inside a polymer matrix, using external stimuli such as magnetic fields and acoustic waves to steer that organisation and produce materials with specific nanoparticle configurations, which in turn change how soft or brittle the material is.
episodes.image_alt: Alexandra Rosen (Brumberg) on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 185: Raising the stakes - nanoparticle playing cards — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanodetectives revolutionising next generation sensors
episodes.summary: Stephanie Gallant has been active in research since 2014, when a professor whose class she was taking offered her a term in her materials chemistry group at Memorial University in Newfoundland. Her graduate work covered the synthesis, characterisation and application of magnetic semiconductor nanoparticles, where changing the reaction scale produced spheres, disks and other shapes; she is proudest of the cobalt ferrite sensor experiments and the unexpected crystal growth puzzles they threw up.
episodes.image_alt: Steph Gallant on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 184: Nanodetectives revolutionising next generation sensors — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanodetectives revolutionising next generation sensors
episodes.summary: Stephanie Gallant works in vibrational spectroscopy, using light to study materials and their structures, with a focus on plasmonic materials for sensors. Plasmonics uses metals such as gold or silver patterned with nanoscale features, which behave unusually when interacting with light at that size scale; tuning the surface chemistry lets her sensors detect specific dilute analytes at extremely low concentrations in environments such as wastewater or blood.
episodes.image_alt: Steph Gallant on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 183: Nanodetectives revolutionising next generation sensors — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Glowy Things & Why They Glow
episodes.summary: Lea Nienhaus began as a BSc student at the University of Ulm in 2007, took her PhD at UIUC in 2015, and joined Florida State in 2018 after a postdoc at MIT. Her group works with both nanocrystals and bulk semiconductors such as perovskites, correlating optical scanning tunnelling microscopy with optical spectroscopy to understand energy and charge transfer; their perovskite-sensitised upconversion device absorbs low-energy 800 nm red light and emits higher-energy yellow light at 600 nm.
episodes.image_alt: Lea Nienhaus on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 182: Glowy Things & Why They Glow — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Glowy Things & Why They Glow
episodes.summary: Lea Nienhaus and her group work towards using more of the full solar spectrum, by understanding the properties of emerging semiconductors and interconverting wavelengths of light. They investigate how light interacts with matter using a range of spectroscopic and structural characterisation tools, including optical scanning tunnelling microscopy and photon upconversion.
episodes.image_alt: Lea Nienhaus on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 181: Glowy Things & Why They Glow — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Ultra Fast & Furious Spin Dynamics
episodes.summary: Reza Rouzegar started in electrical engineering, learning circuits from DC up through radio and gigahertz frequencies, and worked on metasurfaces during his bachelor's. His research now runs through the core spintronic operations, using ultrafast demagnetisation and terahertz spectroscopy to reach spin voltage and chemical potential; asked what he is proudest of, he answers simply: spin current.
episodes.image_alt: Reza Rouzegar on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 180: Ultra Fast & Furious Spin Dynamics — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Ultra Fast & Furious Spin Dynamics
episodes.summary: Reza Rouzegar works on spintronics and terahertz spectroscopy. Classical electronics uses only the electron's charge to carry information, while spintronics adds its spin, up or down, as a further degree of freedom, which requires being able to turn spins around, transport them and detect them; one common application is storage, where the bits zero and one map onto spin up and spin down.
episodes.image_alt: Reza Rouzegar on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 179: Ultra Fast & Furious Spin Dynamics — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Electrifying science
episodes.affiliation: Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Energy and Climate Research IEK-12: Helmholtz Institute Münster
episodes.summary: Kerstin Neuhaus started out studying Earth sciences at Münster because she was fascinated by volcanoes and space, fell in love with microscopy along the way, and moved towards materials science. Her work now centres on atomic force microscopy and on developing AFM-based electrochemical methods to measure transport processes in real-life materials; her bachelor thesis studied weathering behaviour on samples of the El Hammami meteorite.
episodes.image_alt: Kerstin Neuhaus on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 178: Electrifying science — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Electrifying science
episodes.affiliation: Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Institute of Energy and Climate Research IEK-12: Helmholtz Institute Münster
episodes.summary: Kerstin Neuhaus uses a small conductive tip to measure charge transport characteristics and image transport processes at the interfaces inside energy materials. Those interfaces can be grain boundaries in single-phase or dual-phase ceramics, or interphase boundaries in polymer-ceramic composites.
episodes.image_alt: Kerstin Neuhaus on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 177: Electrifying science — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Lasagna à la Nano
episodes.summary: Jarrett Dillenburger has always been curious about science but also loves history, and both subjects have shaped him; a general chemistry course at Denison University convinced him of how effectively chemistry explains the world. He focuses on the chemistry of inorganic two-dimensional materials, particularly the synthesis and characterisation of nanosheets derived from transition metal dichalcogenides.
episodes.image_alt: Jarrett Dillenburger on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 176: Lasagna à la Nano — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Lasagna à la Nano
episodes.summary: Jarrett Dillenburger explores fundamental questions in the chemistry of layered inorganic solids and the nanomaterials derived from them, including how nanosheets are functionalised and exfoliated and the thermochemistry behind those processes. The episode also covers the synthesis methods used to make nanomaterials from layered materials.
episodes.image_alt: Jarrett Dillenburger on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 175: Lasagna à la Nano — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Surface chemistry reactions make nanomaterials happy
episodes.summary: Sakiru Abiodun is Nigerian, took his bachelor's and master's at the University of Ibadan in 2014 and 2017, and began his PhD in 2018. His recent paper uses isothermal titration calorimetry alongside a complementary NMR study to understand how quaternary ammonium halide ligands behave on the surface of halide perovskite quantum dots.
episodes.image_alt: Sakiru Abiodun on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 174: Surface chemistry reactions make nanomaterials happy — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Surface chemistry reactions make nanomaterials happy
episodes.summary: Sakiru Abiodun explores the surface chemistry of colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals, better known as quantum dots. His work aims to improve the stability and the optical and electronic properties of halide perovskite quantum dots for a range of optoelectronic applications.
episodes.image_alt: Sakiru Abiodun on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 173: Surface chemistry reactions make nanomaterials happy — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Everything SAXS - Big Methods for Small Studies
episodes.affiliation: BAM Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing
episodes.summary: Brian Pauw came through a master's in chemical engineering at Eindhoven, an internship at Teijin Aramid doing X-ray scattering on fibres, a computational chemistry project on metal hydrides, and a PhD at DTU in Denmark. The structures X-ray scattering can measure run from 0.3 to 400 nanometres, so as he puts it, it is all nano underneath; he counts reimagining the data corrections for X-ray scattering among his biggest achievements.
episodes.image_alt: Brian R. Pauw on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 172: Everything SAXS - Big Methods for Small Studies — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Everything SAXS - Big Methods for Small Studies
episodes.affiliation: BAM Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing
episodes.summary: Brian Pauw argues that intelligent material development requires understanding a material's fine structure and how that structure produces its behaviour. He traces the structure back from how X-rays scatter on their way through a material, an old technique whose accuracy and reliability have improved drastically in recent years.
episodes.image_alt: Brian R. Pauw on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 171: Everything SAXS - Big Methods for Small Studies — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Argon Through the Looking Glass
episodes.summary: Rebecca Cummings did her undergraduate physics degree at the University of Kent, took on a materials project for her master's, and is now near the end of a PhD at Glasgow. Her first paper used electron energy loss spectroscopy to count the argon atoms inside tiny bubbles in a sample, a technique she has since applied to other materials.
episodes.image_alt: Rebecca Cummings on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 170: Argon Through the Looking Glass — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Argon Through the Looking Glass
episodes.summary: Rebecca Cummings is an electron microscopist working with electron energy loss spectroscopy, firing electrons through a sample and reading its structure and elemental composition from the way they emerge. She mostly studies the mirror coatings of gravitational wave detectors, where understanding the structure of the coatings helps make the detectors more sensitive.
episodes.image_alt: Rebecca Cummings on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 169: Argon Through the Looking Glass — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Breaking Barriers using Smart Materials
episodes.summary: Yonatan Calahorra's research career began nearly fifteen years ago studying the mechanical properties of silicon nanowires for an MSc at the Technion, followed by a PhD in another lab there. He now studies how processing, composition and size control a material's functional properties, such as how piezoelectricity manifests at the nanoscale and how to measure it; among his projects are highly sensitive piezotronic pressure sensors based on GaAs.
episodes.image_alt: Yonatan Calahorra on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 168: Breaking Barriers using Smart Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Breaking Barriers using Smart Materials
episodes.summary: Yonatan Calahorra works on the coupling of functional properties in smart or multifunctional materials, and in particular the magneto-electro-mechanical coupling triangle. That takes very different forms depending on the properties, scale and material involved, from GaN-based LEDs to the mechanical manipulation of macromolecular order in bacterial cellulose.
episodes.image_alt: Yonatan Calahorra on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 167: Breaking Barriers using Smart Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Filming Electronic Movies in Emergent Phases
episodes.affiliation: Fritz Haber Institute of the Max Planck Society
episodes.summary: Chris Nicholson started in Scotland at St Andrews, did his PhD in Berlin and a postdoc in Switzerland before returning to Berlin as a group leader. His interest is fundamental material behaviour, and he points to projects built from the ground up around bands, bonds and strain.
episodes.image_alt: Chris Nicholson on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 166: Filming Electronic Movies in Emergent Phases — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Filming Electronic Movies in Emergent Phases
episodes.affiliation: Fritz Haber Institute of the Max Planck Society
episodes.summary: Chris Nicholson studies how electrons behave in solids, where huge numbers of them jostle together inside a crystal and produce a range of exciting collective behaviours. His goal is to understand the mechanisms behind that behaviour and then modify it controllably, by investigating both electronic structure, how electrons organise, and dynamics, how they exchange energy.
episodes.image_alt: Chris Nicholson on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 165: Filming Electronic Movies in Emergent Phases — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Artifical intelligence meets nanoscience
episodes.affiliation: Department of Chemistry, University of Copenhagen
episodes.summary: Andy Sode Anker is part of a group synthesising new functional materials, travelling to synchrotrons to probe their atomic structure with intense X-ray beams generated by electrons moving at close to the speed of light. The measurements produce enormous datasets, which he analyses using artificial intelligence.
episodes.image_alt: Andy Soder Anke on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 196: Artifical intelligence meets nanoscience — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Phase Change Materials-from DVDs to Tunable Photonics
episodes.affiliation: at ETH Zurich until end of March, at TU Eindhoven from May on
episodes.summary: Ann-Katrin Michel left school in Germany in 2005 for RWTH Aachen, among the first German universities to offer a BSc/MSc programme. She works on understanding phase-change materials and their size-dependent properties, and on reversibly switching their structural state; she was among the first to publish on phase-change materials for tunable photonics.
episodes.image_alt: Ann-Katrin Michel on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 112: Phase Change Materials-from DVDs to Tunable Photonics — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Phase Change Materials-from DVDs to Tunable Photonics
episodes.affiliation: at ETH Zurich until end of March, at TU Eindhoven from May on
episodes.summary: Ann-Katrin Michel works on phase-change materials, which differ structurally between their amorphous and crystalline states, a contrast that shifts their refractive index and changes electrical resistivity by up to five orders of magnitude. Those properties are used for data storage and active photonics; her focus is the latter, and most recently phase-change material nanoparticles.
episodes.image_alt: Ann-Katrin Michel on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 111: Phase Change Materials-from DVDs to Tunable Photonics — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: A Nanomaterials Patchwork
episodes.summary: Andrea Armani's route ran from Memphis to the University of Chicago, then Caltech, and on to USC, where she is Professor of Chemical Engineering and Materials Science. She makes new nanomaterials for photonics, and when asked which project she is proudest of, says there are so many that it depends on the day.
episodes.image_alt: Andrea Armani on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 164: A Nanomaterials Patchwork — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: A Nanomaterials Patchwork
episodes.summary: Andrea Armani develops new materials for optics and diagnostics. The episode is given over largely to careers and advice, interesting science, and answering questions as they come up.
episodes.image_alt: Andrea Armani on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 163: A Nanomaterials Patchwork — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Revolutionising Optics with New Materials
episodes.summary: Hongyan Mei started research in nanophotonics during her sophomore year at Zhejiang University, where she majored in optical science and engineering and was able to join a group working on nanofibres. Her materials are mostly at the micro and nanoscale, and her characterisation methods let her investigate them at the nanoscale; she singles out the focused ion beam work on engineering optical materials.
episodes.image_alt: Mei Hongyan on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 162: Revolutionising Optics with New Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Revolutionising Optics with New Materials
episodes.summary: Hongyan Mei engineers and characterises complex optical systems, developing advanced optical characterisation methods to investigate difficult optical materials. That work produced the discovery of a new material system, transition metal chalcogenides, with giant optical anisotropy; a second strand uses a commercial focused ion beam to locally modulate the optical properties of metal oxides through ion doping and defect engineering.
episodes.image_alt: Mei Hongyan on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 161: Revolutionising Optics with New Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Dancing Atoms and the Stories They Tell
episodes.summary: Burak Guzelturk trained as an electrical and electronics engineer, was amazed by nanoscience, and did his MSc and PhD on nanomaterials and photonic devices before a postdoc that took him into terahertz spectroscopy and ultrafast structural measurement. His speciality is advanced characterisation: time-resolved X-ray diffraction with sub-nanosecond resolution following a laser pulse. He is proudest of his PhD work developing colloidal nanoplatelet lasers.
episodes.image_alt: Burak Guzelturk on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 160: Dancing Atoms and the Stories They Tell — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Dancing Atoms and the Stories They Tell
episodes.summary: Burak Guzelturk is a beamline scientist at the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratory, having started out synthesising semiconductor nanocrystals and building photonic devices from them. He now excites nanomaterials with femtosecond and picosecond laser pulses and watches the atoms move afterwards, revealing how materials convert light into electricity and heat, which matters for solar energy and photocatalysis.
episodes.image_alt: Burak Guzelturk on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 159: Dancing Atoms and the Stories They Tell — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nature Inspired Additive Manufacturing
episodes.summary: Hortense Le Ferrand was educated in France, took an MSc in materials in Switzerland and did her thesis in tissue engineering at Imperial College London before returning to ETH Zurich. Her work is entirely materials-focused, developing polymer, natural and ceramic composites; she is proudest of her morphing composites, where microstructure control drives shape change across a wide range of materials.
episodes.image_alt: Hortense Le Ferrand on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 158: Nature Inspired Additive Manufacturing — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nature Inspired Additive Manufacturing
episodes.summary: Hortense Le Ferrand combines additive manufacturing with the self- or directed assembly of microparticles to create composite materials with enhanced properties. She works out how the local orientation of those microparticles governs macroscopic mechanical and functional behaviour, in tough ceramic composites, electrodes with higher energy storage and morphing composites.
episodes.image_alt: Hortense Le Ferrand on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 157: Nature Inspired Additive Manufacturing — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Creating New Quantum Materials Atom by Atom
episodes.affiliation: Depeartment of Physics, University of Cambridge
episodes.summary: Tiffany Harte decided she wanted to be a physicist after reading Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials trilogy as a teenager, and studied physics at the University of St Andrews. She places her own work at the edge of the traditional nanoscience domain, using gases of atoms cooled until their quantum statistics dominate and controlled precisely with magnetic and optical fields; her final-year undergraduate project was the first research she truly owned.
episodes.image_alt: Tiffany Harte on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 156: Creating New Quantum Materials Atom by Atom — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Creating New Quantum Materials Atom by Atom
episodes.affiliation: Depeartment of Physics, University of Cambridge
episodes.summary: Tiffany Harte cools atoms to less than a millionth of a degree above absolute zero and uses them to study complex phenomena. Trapping atoms in patterns of laser light lets her build experimental simulations of complicated materials and probe effects that are hard to calculate or measure directly; her new experiment will use ultracold atom clouds as a detector for dark matter and gravitational waves.
episodes.image_alt: Tiffany Harte on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 155: Creating New Quantum Materials Atom by Atom — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Materials Science – Hot from the Press
episodes.summary: Giulia Pacchioni is a Senior Editor at Nature Reviews Materials, where she shapes review articles from initial idea through peer review to publication, identifying promising topics and helping authors sharpen their structure and figures. She reached editing after a physics PhD at EPFL using scanning tunnelling microscopy to study how molecules self-assemble on surfaces, and helped launch both Nature Reviews Materials and Nature Reviews Physics.
episodes.image_alt: Giulia Pacchioni on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 154: Materials Science – Hot from the Press — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Materials Science – Hot from the Press
episodes.summary: Giulia Pacchioni is a Senior Editor at Nature Reviews Materials, where she shapes review articles from initial idea through peer review to publication, identifying promising topics and helping authors sharpen their structure and figures. She reached editing after a physics PhD at EPFL using scanning tunnelling microscopy to study how molecules self-assemble on surfaces, and helped launch both Nature Reviews Materials and Nature Reviews Physics.
episodes.image_alt: Giulia Pacchioni on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 153: Materials Science – Hot from the Press — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Getting in Shape: Spinning for Nanographene
episodes.summary: Niklas Friedrich took his BSc and MSc in physics in Aachen and Santiago before a PhD in Donostia. His work spans surface science, organic electronics, quantum chemistry and fundamental physics; his first first-author paper made the cover of Physical Review Letters.
episodes.image_alt: Niklas Friedrich on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 152: Getting in Shape: Spinning for Nanographene — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Getting in Shape: Spinning for Nanographene
episodes.summary: Niklas Friedrich creates flat molecular structures one atom thick, built mostly from hexagons of carbon atoms and designed to be magnetic. One way to make these nanographenes magnetic is to give them a particular shape; he then looks at and inside single nanographenes with a helium-cooled scanning tunnelling microscope to identify which forms of magnetism appear.
episodes.image_alt: Niklas Friedrich on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 151: Getting in Shape: Spinning for Nanographene — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Discoveries at the Interfaces
episodes.affiliation: National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), CO, US
episodes.summary: Ahmad Kirmani did his undergraduate physics degree at Aligarh Muslim University in India before joining the first cohort of graduate students in his research group at KAUST in Saudi Arabia. His PhD explored solar cells based on nanocrystals and he has since zoomed out to bulk perovskites; he demonstrated the first scalable ambient fabrication of a nanocrystal-based solar cell in 2018 and of metal oxide transistors in 2020.
episodes.image_alt: Ahmad Kirmani on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 150: Discoveries at the Interfaces — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Discoveries at the Interfaces
episodes.affiliation: National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), CO, US
episodes.summary: Ahmad Kirmani works on scaling up thin-film optoelectronics, since moving ink-based semiconductor optoelectronics from lab to factory demands a much deeper understanding of the scale-up process itself. He combines interfacial and structural characterisation to enable that transition, and is currently working towards launching perovskite photovoltaics beyond Earth as a space solar technology.
episodes.image_alt: Ahmad Kirmani on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 149: Discoveries at the Interfaces — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Think Magnetically – Materials Around You
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Science and Technology (IST) Austria
episodes.summary: Muhammad Nauman began his academic journey in Ziarat Kaka Sahib, a small town in north-east Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, and went on to a PhD in South Korea after teaching at both high school and university level. His work sits close to magnetism, electronic transport and the thermodynamics of materials, studying micron-sized single crystals that host new physics; his PhD examined magnetic anisotropy in single-crystal strontium iridate.
episodes.image_alt: Muhammad Nauman on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 148: Think Magnetically – Materials Around You — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Think Magnetically – Materials Around You
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Science and Technology (IST) Austria
episodes.summary: Muhammad Nauman studies microscale quantum materials under extreme conditions: temperatures nearly 300 degrees below room temperature and magnetic fields as high as 100 tesla. Under those conditions the materials display phenomena such as superconductivity, Majorana fermions and multipole ordering.
episodes.image_alt: Muhammad Nauman on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 147: Think Magnetically – Materials Around You — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Magic of plasma and thin films
episodes.summary: Karyn Jarvis says she fell into science rather than choosing it, never having been one of those children who played with chemistry sets. Her research mixes materials and nanoscience, modifying surface properties with nanometre-thin films, because a surface governs how a material interacts with its environment, as with a hip implant; her first postdoc project was the most productive and most instructive of her career.
episodes.image_alt: Karyn Jarvis on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 146: Magic of plasma and thin films — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Magic of plasma and thin films
episodes.summary: Karyn Jarvis works on surface modification and thin film deposition, laying down coatings only nanometres thick to give a surface the properties required. She has used such modified surfaces to deliver drugs, remove water contaminants, protect solar cells and control how biomaterials interact with bacteria and cells.
episodes.image_alt: Karyn Jarvis on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 145: Magic of plasma and thin films — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Punching Materials Until They Get Angry
episodes.summary: Yolanda Manzanares studied physics at UAM, fell for scanning probe microscopy while imaging graphene moires with STM for her final project, then moved to AFM in air for her master's because it felt more hands-on. She studies and manipulates flakes of material at the nanometre scale, including measuring the toughness of MoS2 nanodrums, micron-sized holes covered by a single layer of material.
episodes.image_alt: Yolanda Manzanares on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 144: Punching Materials Until They Get Angry — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Punching Materials Until They Get Angry
episodes.summary: Yolanda Manzanares studies 2D materials, those that can be thinned down to layers even a single atom thick, using atomic force microscopy. She prepares samples with different characteristics and observes what happens when high pressure is applied to them with a very sharp tip controlled to nanometre precision.
episodes.image_alt: Yolanda Manzanares on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 143: Punching Materials Until They Get Angry — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Benefits of Noise
episodes.summary: Said Rodriguez has worked across a range of nanoscale systems over the years, from nano-antennas to quantum dots and cavities containing semiconductor quantum wells. He is driven mainly by fundamental physics questions but leans heavily on nanomaterials to pursue them; a recent paper from his group demonstrates how to turn noise into an advantage for signal detection.
episodes.image_alt: Said Rahimzadeh-Kalaleh Rodriguez on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 142: Benefits of Noise — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Benefits of Noise
episodes.summary: Said Rodriguez is interested in how light behaves at the nanoscale, how it interacts with matter, and the phenomena that emerge from that interaction, including the superfluidity of light. He has worked on metallic nano-antennas, semiconductor cavities and, as a group leader, the deliberately odd idea of filling tiny cavities with olive oil, and is also interested in the potential benefits of noise for nanoscale optical systems.
episodes.image_alt: Said Rahimzadeh-Kalaleh Rodriguez on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 141: Benefits of Noise — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Electron Dances in Atomically Thin Crystals
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Photonics and Quantum Sciences, Heriot-Watt University
episodes.summary: Servet Ozdemir took a BSc and integrated MPhys at Warwick before a PhD at Manchester's Graphene NOWNANO Centre for Doctoral Training. He works on a relatively newly discovered class of materials running from graphene to transition metal dichalcogenides and beyond, and carried out the first systematic experimental investigation of rhombohedral graphite thin films.
episodes.image_alt: Servet Ozdemir on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 140: Electron Dances in Atomically Thin Crystals — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Electron Dances in Atomically Thin Crystals
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Photonics and Quantum Sciences, Heriot-Watt University
episodes.summary: Servet Ozdemir works on atomically thin two-dimensional crystals, atoms arranged in honeycomb patterns that show fascinating manifestations of quantum physics. He probes them with two complementary approaches, electron transport and light, and the episode includes a short history of how the 2D materials field came about.
episodes.image_alt: Servet Ozdemir on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 139: Electron Dances in Atomically Thin Crystals — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: If you Want to Write a Nanonovel: Scanning Probe Lithography
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Optoelectronics and Microtechnology Systems (Politechnic University of Madrid)
episodes.summary: Yu Kyoung Ryu took a physics degree at Universidad Complutense de Madrid, worked on ZnO during her master's and did her PhD on oxidation scanning probe lithography. She is now exploring graphene for energy storage and harvesting devices aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals and the European Green Deal; at IBM Zurich she produced silicon nanowires under 10 nanometres wide.
episodes.image_alt: Yu Kyoung Ryu on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 138: If you Want to Write a Nanonovel: Scanning Probe Lithography — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Using Strain to Control 2D Materials ft. Aki Pulkkinen & Chris Nicholson | Lucia | #7 #InOtherWords
episodes.lead: Using Strain to Control 2D Materials ft. Aki Pulkkinen & Chris Nicholson | Lucia | #7 #InOtherWords
episodes.affiliation: Host: Lucia Rotheray · Guest: Chris Nicholson, Aki Pulkkinen
episodes.summary: Postdocs Aki Pulkkinen and Chris Nicholson, from the Ultrafast Spectroscopy group at the University of Fribourg, explain how they use mechanical strain to manipulate materials, working together as theorist and experimentalist on a uniaxial strain-induced phase transition in a 2D topological semimetal.

episodes.title: If you Want to Write a Nanonovel: Scanning Probe Lithography
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Optoelectronics and Microtechnology Systems (Politechnic University of Madrid)
episodes.summary: Yu Kyoung Ryu is an expert in scanning probe lithography, using an atomic force microscope as a fabrication tool that can pattern structures below 10 nanometres in almost any material, from semiconductors to polymers and biological samples. She also fabricates and characterises optoelectronic devices from 2D materials, and the episode makes the case for the AFM as far more than an imaging instrument.
episodes.image_alt: Yu Kyoung Ryu on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 137: If you Want to Write a Nanonovel: Scanning Probe Lithography — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanoscale Energy Transport: The Motion Picture
episodes.affiliation: Condensed Matter Physics Center, Universidad Autonoma de Madrid
episodes.summary: Ferry Prins studied synthetic chemistry at Leiden University and began in molecular magnetism before moving steadily towards physics. His group specialises in nanomaterial spectroscopy and transient microscopy, which lets them visualise carrier transport in semiconductors, effectively making short films of energy carriers moving through perovskite semiconductors.
episodes.image_alt: Ferry Prins on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 136: Nanoscale Energy Transport: The Motion Picture — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanoscale Energy Transport: The Motion Picture
episodes.affiliation: Condensed Matter Physics Center, Universidad Autonoma de Madrid
episodes.summary: Ferry Prins and his group work on understanding and controlling the optoelectronic properties of nanostructured materials and devices. Because these materials are so far from perfect there are a thousand ways to lose optical energy along the way, so they combine material development with time-resolved microscopy and spectroscopy to stop it escaping.
episodes.image_alt: Ferry Prins on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 135: Nanoscale Energy Transport: The Motion Picture — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Poker phases of perovskites
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Advanced Materials (INAM) at Universidad Jaume I, Castellón de la Plana, Spain
episodes.summary: Sofia Masi chose chemistry after a secondary-school class that, as she puts it, did something to her, and studied in Pisa before a PhD at CNR Nanotec. She frames nanoscience as the scale at which quantum mechanical and surface boundary effects start to dominate; perovskite solar cells are the most promising next-generation photovoltaic technology, and their low stability in ambient conditions is the limitation she works on.
episodes.image_alt: Sofia Masi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 134: Poker phases of perovskites — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Poker phases of perovskites
episodes.affiliation: Institute of Advanced Materials (INAM) at Universidad Jaume I, Castellón de la Plana, Spain
episodes.summary: Sofia Masi works on perovskite devices, solar cells and LEDs, covering structural and optoelectronic properties, electrical characterisation and synthesis. Her current focus is thermodynamically stabilising unstable photoactive perovskite crystal phases through chemi-structural interaction with inorganic quantum dots, to improve the efficiency and ambient stability of both material and device.
episodes.image_alt: Sofia Masi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 133: Poker phases of perovskites — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Shaking Atomic Lattices with Strong Laser Pulses
episodes.affiliation: Fritz Haber Institute of the Max Planck Society (Germany)
episodes.summary: Sebastian Maehrlein studied physics at Konstanz, became interested in laser and semiconductor physics, and spent a few months at a laser company's research lab in California. His work targets the dynamics and transient states of materials rather than their static properties, and a large part of it is building the state-of-the-art laser tools required; during his PhD he demonstrated a new nonlinear mechanism for driving Raman-active lattice vibrations.
episodes.image_alt: Sebastian Maehrlein on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 132: Shaking Atomic Lattices with Strong Laser Pulses — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Shaking Atomic Lattices with Strong Laser Pulses
episodes.affiliation: Fritz Haber Institute of the Max Planck Society (Germany)
episodes.summary: Sebastian Maehrlein points out that, contrary to what the podcast title suggests, his group is concerned with the ultrafast dynamics of structures rather than resolving them in space. They generate intense, phase-stable laser pulses in the terahertz and mid-infrared range to coherently drive specific lattice vibrations, controlling material properties on demand and hunting for new transient phases of solids.
episodes.image_alt: Sebastian Maehrlein on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 131: Shaking Atomic Lattices with Strong Laser Pulses — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Embracing Change – Materials for Greener Tomorrow
episodes.summary: William Brant traces his path back to a childhood obsession with gemstones and minerals and a decent rock collection at home. A chemist who specialised in crystallography, he now studies how materials form during synthesis and change during use in electrochemical devices; he is proudest of work synthesising Prussian white, a cathode material.
episodes.image_alt: William Brant on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 130: Embracing Change – Materials for Greener Tomorrow — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Embracing Change – Materials for Greener Tomorrow
episodes.summary: William Brant uses X-rays and neutrons to understand how functional materials form and change, in particular the electrochemically active materials found in batteries. He describes it as X-ray vision for seeing inside a battery and working out which atomic-scale features lead to better performance.
episodes.image_alt: William Brant on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 129: Embracing Change – Materials for Greener Tomorrow — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nano Fun with AFM (Atomic Force Microscopy)
episodes.affiliation: Condensed Matter Physics Department, Autonomous University of Madrid
episodes.summary: Pablo Ares took his physics degrees in Madrid and then spent years at Nanotec Electronica, a company designing and commercialising scanning probe microscopes, before returning to academia. Scanning probe techniques have run through his entire career; he led the worldwide experimental effort behind the first isolation of antimonene, a 2D material one antimony atom thick.
episodes.image_alt: Pablo Ares on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 128: Nano Fun with AFM (Atomic Force Microscopy) — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nano Fun with AFM (Atomic Force Microscopy)
episodes.affiliation: Condensed Matter Physics Department, Autonomous University of Madrid
episodes.summary: Pablo Ares works both on advancing the atomic force microscopy technique itself and on the fundamental science of low-dimensional materials: the basic properties of 2D materials, how they combine into van der Waals heterostructures, and the electrical properties of molecules under extreme confinement.
episodes.image_alt: Pablo Ares on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 127: Nano Fun with AFM (Atomic Force Microscopy) — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Who Performs Better Under High Pressure – Humans or Perovskites?
episodes.summary: Loreta Muscarella studied chemistry and physical chemistry in Rome before an Erasmus placement took her to the Netherlands for her master's thesis, where she stayed. Many of the mechanisms governing how perovskites behave are still not well defined, which is what her work sets out to pin down; she is proudest of a physics project she never expected to be able to tackle as a chemist by training.
episodes.image_alt: Loreta Muscarella on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 126: Who Performs Better Under High Pressure – Humans or Perovskites? — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Who Performs Better Under High Pressure – Humans or Perovskites?
episodes.summary: Loreta Muscarella works on perovskite thin films, a new class of material that is extremely promising for solar cells, LEDs, thermoelectric devices and lasers. She characterises their properties to establish the conditions that give optimal performance in each of those applications.
episodes.image_alt: Loreta Muscarella on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 125: Who Performs Better Under High Pressure – Humans or Perovskites? — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: A Secret Key to Unlock the Protein Nanocages
episodes.summary: Andrew Care did a BSc and MSc in biological sciences in New Zealand, working in animal vaccine production and as a lab manager, before a PhD in Sydney that started on biofuels and became something else entirely. His work is on biologically derived materials, genetically reprogramming natural proteins to do new jobs; his group's first paper bioengineered a bacterial protein organelle to mediate photodynamic therapy.
episodes.image_alt: Andrew  Care on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 124: A Secret Key to Unlock the Protein Nanocages — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: A Secret Key to Unlock the Protein Nanocages
episodes.summary: Andrew Care takes proteins away from their everyday jobs and reprograms them for non-natural applications such as cancer therapy. His group re-engineered encapsulins, tiny protein nanoparticles that serve as organelles inside bacteria, for photodynamic therapy, and studies how protein nanoparticles self-assemble and package cargo.
episodes.image_alt: Andrew  Care on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 123: A Secret Key to Unlock the Protein Nanocages — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Magnetism through the Eyes of Racing Neutrons
episodes.summary: Johanna Jochum studied physics at ETH Zurich, working on iron pnictide superconductors for her master's thesis before a year in metal physics and a PhD on nanoscale systems. She is candid that nano has taken a back seat in her current role, because neutrons interact so weakly that nanoscale samples are very hard to measure, and about how lost she felt on joining a field and an instrument that were both new to her.
episodes.image_alt: Johanna Jochum on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 122: Magnetism through the Eyes of Racing Neutrons — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Magnetism through the Eyes of Racing Neutrons
episodes.summary: Johanna Jochum is instrument scientist on RESEDA, a neutron resonant spin-echo spectrometer optimised for magnetic materials. Most of its experiments measure dynamic processes: how the magnetic spins of iron behave close to the transition from ferromagnetism to paramagnetism, or how fast vortices move inside superconductors.
episodes.image_alt: Johanna Jochum on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 121: Magnetism through the Eyes of Racing Neutrons — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: The Magic of Nanocrystals
episodes.summary: Andrew Pun got into nanoscience early, starting research at the Molecular Foundry at Berkeley National Lab as an undergraduate before a PhD at Columbia on organic electronics. He sees nanocrystals as the heart of nanoscience, the clearest demonstration of the interesting properties that emerge at very small scales; his proudest project applied triplet upconversion, known from organic materials chemistry, to a new problem.
episodes.image_alt: Andrew Pun on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 120: The Magic of Nanocrystals — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: The Magic of Nanocrystals
episodes.summary: Andrew Pun works on nanocrystals, crystals only nanometres across, in which electrons and holes are confined to far less space than they would like. That quantum confinement gives them all sorts of interesting properties; his focus is magic-sized nanocrystals, so called because only certain sizes can be grown.
episodes.image_alt: Andrew Pun on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 119: The Magic of Nanocrystals — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Melting Ice with Very Expensive Lasers
episodes.summary: Marjorie Ladd Parada studied food technology in Mexico and worked in industry R&D before deciding she needed more mental stimulation and moving abroad for a master's. She now works on amorphous ice, the most common form of ice in the universe, using X-rays to resolve its structure at the nanometre scale.
episodes.image_alt: Marjorie Ladd Parada on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 118: Melting Ice with Very Expensive Lasers — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Melting Ice with Very Expensive Lasers
episodes.summary: Marjorie Ladd Parada studies the structure and dynamics of amorphous ice and supercooled water at large X-ray facilities, and sometimes shoots lasers at them too. The episode also covers her route into the field, life as a postdoc, and writing grant proposals.
episodes.image_alt: Marjorie Ladd Parada on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 117: Melting Ice with Very Expensive Lasers — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: 2D Materials – to Twist or Not to Twist
episodes.summary: El-Abed Haidar's academic route began in 2009 at Lebanon's most competitive engineering faculty, an attempt that collapsed early before he found his footing. As a computational materials scientist he now studies carbon-based nanoelectronic devices, both to understand their properties and to predict new device materials and structures.
episodes.image_alt: El-abed Haidar on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 116: 2D Materials – to Twist or Not to Twist — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: 2D Materials – to Twist or Not to Twist
episodes.summary: El-Abed Haidar uses first-principles quantum mechanical calculations to identify promising carbon-based structures for the nanotechnology industry, including moletronics, sensors, semiconductors and superconductors. The episode covers how that computational work is done and the conferences he has taken it to.
episodes.image_alt: El-abed Haidar on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 115: 2D Materials – to Twist or Not to Twist — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Defects Make Better Devices
episodes.summary: Robert Karsthof studied physics in Leipzig and joined the semiconductor physics group at the end of his bachelor's degree. He argues that in semiconductors everything interesting happens at the nanoscale, from crystals built atom by atom to the point defects that determine how a device behaves; nickel oxide, versatile and difficult, has stayed with him since his PhD.
episodes.image_alt: Robert Karsthof on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 114: Defects Make Better Devices — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Defects Make Better Devices
episodes.summary: Robert Karsthof studies defects in semiconductor crystals, the places where an atom is missing or swapped, which have an outsized effect on the properties behind smartphones, solar cells and LEDs. The episode covers what crystal defects are, why they matter, and the experimental methods used to detect and characterise them.
episodes.image_alt: Robert Karsthof on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 113: Defects Make Better Devices — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: The Curious Case of Melting at the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Laia Delgado Callico studied chemistry in Barcelona, came to London on an Erasmus grant and stayed for a master's in molecular biophysics and then a PhD. Her computational work on metallic nanoparticles sits between materials science, physics and chemistry; her first first-author paper identified a universal signature in how metallic nanoparticles melt.
episodes.image_alt: Laia Delgado Callico on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 110: The Curious Case of Melting at the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: The Curious Case of Melting at the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Laia Delgado Callico studies how the shape and size of metallic nanoparticles change their physical and chemical properties, analysing vibrational modes and electronic structure to understand their stability and their interaction with noble gases. She also developed a new method to explain why identically sized particles of different shapes melt at different temperatures.
episodes.image_alt: Laia Delgado Callico on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 109: The Curious Case of Melting at the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Puppeteer Playing with 2D Materials
episodes.summary: Anna Piras took a bachelor's and master's in chemistry at Bologna before moving to Heidelberg for a PhD in computational chemistry. She is deriving the structure-property relationships that govern carbon-based nanomaterials, with the aim of rationally designing sensors for contaminants and dangerous compounds.
episodes.image_alt: Anna Piras on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 108: Puppeteer Playing with 2D Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Puppeteer Playing with 2D Materials
episodes.summary: Anna Piras computationally models the non-covalent interactions in graphene-based and other nanomaterials, for use in molecular electronics and catalysis. Her work connects properties that can be simulated on a computer to how those materials actually perform in experiments.
episodes.image_alt: Anna Piras on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 107: Puppeteer Playing with 2D Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Strange World of Quantum Materials
episodes.summary: Otto Mustonen works on quantum materials, focusing on quantum spin liquids in which the tiny magnetic spins behave like a liquid even at absolute zero. He probes them using neutrons and muons, and the episode also covers what it is like to run experiments at large neutron facilities.
episodes.image_alt: Otto Mustonen on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 105: Strange World of Quantum Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Strange World of Quantum Materials
episodes.summary: Otto Mustonen did his PhD on magnetism in strongly correlated oxides at Aalto University and describes himself, for all the physics techniques he uses, as a materials chemist whose main job is designing and synthesising new materials. He points to quantum spin liquids as the payoff: an exotic state predicted by Philip Anderson thirty years ago that could underpin a new kind of quantum computer.
episodes.image_alt: Otto Mustonen on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 106: Strange World of Quantum Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Building Microscopes for Fun & Health
episodes.summary: Kwasi Kwakwa came to imaging science through a physics undergraduate degree, a masters in bio/nanophotonics and a PhD imaging the orientation of single molecules. He now images fluorescently labelled RNA strands inside human cells at the nanometre scale, and counts it a career highlight that microscope ideas from his first postdoc are used beyond his own lab.
episodes.image_alt: Kwasi Kwakwa on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 104: Building Microscopes for Fun & Health — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Building Microscopes for Fun & Health
episodes.summary: Kwasi Kwakwa builds and manages the microscopes used to image active genes in thin slices of tissue. The episode covers an introduction to microscopy and fluorescence, what a day in the lab actually looks like, and race and diversity in science.
episodes.image_alt: Kwasi Kwakwa on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 103: Building Microscopes for Fun & Health — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Stretching Atomically Thin Materials
episodes.summary: Andres Castellanos-Gomez was a tenure-track researcher at IMDEA Nanoscience before winning a tenured position at CSIC through its selection committee process. He has worked on 2D materials since the beginning of his PhD, changing his experimental tools and what he measures over the years but never leaving that class of nanomaterial; in 2017 he won an ERC Starting Grant to fabricate optoelectronic devices.
episodes.image_alt: Andres Castellanos-Gomez on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 100: Stretching Atomically Thin Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Stretching Atomically Thin Materials
episodes.summary: Andres Castellanos-Gomez isolates and characterises new two-dimensional materials, a class of nanomaterial only one or a few atoms thick. His research group is interested in using them in optoelectronic devices and in nanomechanical applications.
episodes.image_alt: Andres Castellanos-Gomez on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 99: Stretching Atomically Thin Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: One Less Dart to Hit the Bullseye
episodes.summary: Jarriaun Streets was pointed towards the field by an undergraduate research advisor who worked with metallic nanoparticles and supervised her senior project on silver nanoparticles, then told her about a master's programme in pharmaceutical nanotechnology at USF. Her work sits in nanomedicine; her master's thesis loaded MPEG-PCL micelles with a drug for better treatment of age-related macular degeneration.
episodes.image_alt: Jarriaun Streets on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 98: One Less Dart to Hit the Bullseye — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: One Less Dart to Hit the Bullseye
episodes.summary: Jarriaun Streets works on MPEG-PCL micelles, whose biocompatibility and nanoscopic size make them promising for sustained drug delivery and release to the posterior segment of the eye.
episodes.image_alt: Jarriaun Streets on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 97: One Less Dart to Hit the Bullseye — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Make Materials Modelling Great Again
episodes.summary: Sherif Abbas left a job as a business analyst for a physics PhD, out of passion for the subject and, he adds, for the Australian visa. He works in computational materials science, and predicted the source of single photon emission in hexagonal boron nitride, which recent papers have since confirmed.
episodes.image_alt: Sherif Abbas on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 96: Make Materials Modelling Great Again — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Make Materials Modelling Great Again
episodes.summary: Sherif Abbas is passionate about the physics and chemistry of 2D materials and how they stretch the boundaries of our understanding of materials and interfaces. Working with experimentalists to explain nanoscale phenomena, he describes it as pushing theory until you sense the cracks in modern physics, and he is after the cracks surrounding the modern explanation of magnetism.
episodes.image_alt: Sherif Abbas on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 95: Make Materials Modelling Great Again — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Electron can take you Anywhere
episodes.summary: Jo Sharp learned about atoms at school aged twelve and has been looking at everything in amazement ever since, pressing the physics and chemistry buttons at every opportunity before reading Natural Sciences at Cambridge. She describes her field as being all over the place, currently mostly alloys and additive manufacturing, where molten metal cools so fast that the resulting microstructure can be genuinely unusual.
episodes.image_alt: Jo Sharp on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 94: Electron can take you Anywhere — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Electron can take you Anywhere
episodes.summary: Jo Sharp is brought pieces of alloy, some used in aircraft engines and some additively manufactured, and works out their micro-scale internal structures. She figures out how to get the information people need, usually with electron microscopes, then makes samples and applies cunning tricks to find the answer.
episodes.image_alt: Jo Sharp on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 93: Electron can take you Anywhere — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: A Chemist's guide to the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Chris Spicer took a roundabout route into materials and nano, starting with a natural sciences undergraduate degree that mixed cell biology, evolution and behaviour with hardcore chemistry. His chemistry is all geared towards making materials with new and interesting properties, manipulating chemicals at the atomic scale alongside biological molecules such as peptides, proteins and carbohydrates; a postdoc in his group found a new way to make materials that conduct electricity like metals while staying soft and flexible.
episodes.image_alt: Chris Spicer on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 92: A Chemist's guide to the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: A Chemist's guide to the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Chris Spicer creates materials for treating or diagnosing disease, ranging from implants that could replace damaged tissue or organs to pregnancy-test-style strips for identifying infections. What unites them is the use of organic chemistry to give the materials novel properties, such as mimicking biological signals or responding to a stimulus like light.
episodes.image_alt: Chris Spicer on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 91: A Chemist's guide to the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Fastest Experiments in the World w/ Electrons & Lasers
episodes.affiliation: University College London, Department of Physics and Astronomy
episodes.summary: Cornelia Hofmann traces her story back to a master's at ETH Zurich, whose loosely organised physics programme let her assemble her own path through the credit system. Attosecond science is above all interested in electron dynamics across bound states of atoms and molecules and, more recently, semiconductors, metallic surfaces and liquids, all under the influence of strong fields.
episodes.image_alt: Cornelia Hofmann on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 90: Fastest Experiments in the World w/ Electrons & Lasers — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Fastest Experiments in the World w/ Electrons & Lasers
episodes.affiliation: University College London, Department of Physics and Astronomy
episodes.summary: Cornelia Hofmann studies how strong, ultrashort laser pulses interact with atoms, in particular strong-field ionisation and what the photoelectrons do next: either flying off and away, or recombining with their parent ion to create high-order harmonic radiation. These processes play out on attosecond and femtosecond timescales.
episodes.image_alt: Cornelia Hofmann on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 89: Fastest Experiments in the World w/ Electrons & Lasers — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanoavengers Assemble!
episodes.summary: Peter Sherrell was interested in science from a young age and chose nanotechnology when picking a degree because it was the new and exciting research field. His work is about unlocking applications by manipulating nanomaterials, from synthesis and defect engineering through to assembly, focused on carbon nanomaterials and 2D materials; he grew structures from two different 2D nanomaterials in a single step, so that they bonded almost perfectly.
episodes.image_alt: Peter Sherrell on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 88: Nanoavengers Assemble! — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanoavengers Assemble!
episodes.summary: Peter Sherrell studies how nanomaterials can be assembled together to build structures with unique properties. That means growing or synthesising nanomaterials directly into 3D structures, probing how different nanomaterials interact with each other, and investigating how they interact with soft systems such as polymers and cells.
episodes.image_alt: Peter Sherrell on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 87: Nanoavengers Assemble! — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Supercool Electrons in 2D Materials
episodes.summary: Antonija Grubisic-Cabo arrived in the field mostly by accident: she did her masters in magnetism and planned to continue, but no PhD positions were available and her supervisor's colleague knew of a project on 2D materials. Her field is the physics of nanomaterials; several 2D materials are expected to underpin future electronics carrying additional bits called spin and valley, which her group probes with circularly polarised laser light.
episodes.image_alt: Antonija Grubisic-Cabo on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 86: Supercool Electrons in 2D Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Supercool Electrons in 2D Materials
episodes.summary: Antonija Grubisic-Cabo studies two-dimensional materials, atomically thin crystals that consist essentially only of surface and therefore behave very differently from their 3D parent compounds. Their properties can be modified by changing the substrate they sit on or the environment around them, and she uses photoemission spectroscopy to study their electronic structure.
episodes.image_alt: Antonija Grubisic-Cabo on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 85: Supercool Electrons in 2D Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Sensing & Killing Bugs - the Nature-inspired Way
episodes.summary: Rajesh Ramanathan has been fascinated by science since wondering as a child how anyone works out which bacterium or virus is making a person ill. One of his primary lines of research makes functional nanoparticles for biomedical applications including sensing and imaging, among them particles that mimic the activity of the natural enzymes driving reactions in the body.
episodes.image_alt: Rajesh Ramanathan on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 84: Sensing & Killing Bugs - the Nature-inspired Way — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Sensing & Killing Bugs - the Nature-inspired Way
episodes.summary: Rajesh Ramanathan uses nanotechnology as a tool for understanding biological phenomena, co-leading the NanoBiotechnology Research Lab. Its core expertise is making unique functional nanoparticles with controlled morphology, surface and optical properties, then using them for diagnostics and sensors that detect biomolecules, pathogens and viruses.
episodes.image_alt: Rajesh Ramanathan on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 83: Sensing & Killing Bugs - the Nature-inspired Way — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Shine Bright like a Nanodiamond
episodes.affiliation: ARC Centre of Excellence for Nanoscale BioPhotonics, School of Science, RMIT University, Melbourne, VIC 3001, Australia
episodes.summary: Emma Wilson came to science and academia the long way round, having worked as a chef and in hospitality for close to two decades, never finished high school and never intended to go to university. Her research blends fundamental nanomaterial science with biological application, from the in vitro work she mostly does through to in vivo and clinical uses; her PhD examines how nanodiamond particle size affects fluorescence properties.
episodes.image_alt: Emma Wilson on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 82: Shine Bright like a Nanodiamond — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Shine Bright like a Nanodiamond
episodes.affiliation: ARC Centre of Excellence for Nanoscale BioPhotonics, School of Science, RMIT University, Melbourne, VIC 3001, Australia
episodes.summary: Emma Wilson works in bionanotechnology, studying nanomaterials at the nano-biological interface and specifically nanosized diamond particles. Nanodiamonds can glow through fluorescence, which allows them to be observed inside living things; she is interested in how particle size affects both their interaction with cells and their ability to glow.
episodes.image_alt: Emma Wilson on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 81: Shine Bright like a Nanodiamond — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Kidney-inspired Nano Brushes for Water Purification
episodes.summary: Halan Mohamed studied chemical engineering as an undergraduate and, as part of the degree, joined the research group she is still in, laying the groundwork for what became her PhD. She modifies the physicochemical properties of polymers at the nanoscale to create better-performing materials; she is proudest of her work on polymer brushes, very aptly named polymer chains that stop unwanted compounds adsorbing.
episodes.image_alt: Halan Mohamed on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 80: Kidney-inspired Nano Brushes for Water Purification — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Kidney-inspired Nano Brushes for Water Purification
episodes.summary: Halan Mohamed takes inspiration from nature to tackle the fouling of surfaces by inorganic compounds such as scale and organic ones such as proteins and oils. She controls the physicochemical properties of surfaces at the nanoscale to make adsorption less likely, aimed at the membrane filters used to purify water.
episodes.image_alt: Halan Mohamed on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 79: Kidney-inspired Nano Brushes for Water Purification — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Uber at Nanoscale to Treat Cancer
episodes.summary: Olivia Geneus wanted to combine science with the health field, and nanomedicine offered exactly that combination. Working in a multifaceted lab, her research overlaps interdisciplinary chemistry with medicine; she developed a nanomedicine agent combining diagnosis and therapy for tumour treatment that also provides MRI of the area.
episodes.image_alt: Olivia Geneus on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 78: Uber at Nanoscale to Treat Cancer — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.summary: Olivia Geneus uses nanoparticles as drug delivery systems, specifically to image and target the regions of a tumour with low oxygen and low pH, which is where resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy tends to arise.
