episodes.title: Nanobits in Water
episodes.summary: Georgina Zimbitas studied surface science and still folds surface and interface work into everything she does, having examined gas-solid, liquid-solid and gas-liquid interfaces and worked on colloidal and micellar systems. She has applied that knowledge in an engineering setting, including modelling surface and near-surface precipitation in binary alloys in order to predict how they behave.
episodes.image_alt: Georgina Zimbitas on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 76: Nanobits in Water — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanobits in Water
episodes.summary: Georgina Zimbitas uses dynamic light scattering and nanoparticle tracking analysis to detect nano-sized entities, ranging from nanoclusters of small organic molecules in aqueous solutions to the critical aggregation concentration of various peptoids.
episodes.image_alt: Georgina Zimbitas on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 75: Nanobits in Water — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: The Brilliance of Smart Materials
episodes.summary: Eleonora D'Elia has been attracted to fun and crazy materials since childhood, when she mixed toothpaste, shaving foam, flour, deodorant and oil in the hope of producing something fantastic. She sees smart materials and composites as bioinspiration made practical, copying plants that move, skin that senses and organs that heal; during her PhD she was funded by DARPA to work on materials that could heal, sense and change shape at the same time.
episodes.image_alt: Eleonora D'Elia on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 74: The Brilliance of Smart Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: The Brilliance of Smart Materials
episodes.summary: Eleonora D'Elia develops smart materials, combining smart polymers with graphene flakes. The results include self-healing structural composites, skin-like materials that sense compression, tension and bending while healing themselves, and shape memory composites and actuators driven purely by the joule heating effect.
episodes.image_alt: Eleonora D'Elia on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 73: The Brilliance of Smart Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Squishy Nanomaterials, their Interactions with Surfaces
episodes.summary: Patrick Spicer works with industry and academic partners to design fluid flow behaviour and performance. Complex fluids contain small amounts of particles, polymers and surfactants and are central to most major products and manufacturing processes; his experiments link fluid structure to flow in order to improve physical modelling.
episodes.image_alt: Patrick Spicer on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 61: Squishy Nanomaterials, their Interactions with Surfaces — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.affiliation: Host: Pranoti Kshirsagar · Guest: Patrick Spicer
episodes.summary: Patrick Spicer explains thunderstorm asthma, a respiratory condition triggered after storms, covering its causes and triggers and the ongoing research into predicting and preventing attacks.

episodes.title: Family Tree of Carbon
episodes.summary: Irene Suarez-Martinez always hated organic chemistry, which she finds ironic given that almost everything she works on is carbon, albeit inorganic; her PhD on graphite was funded by the nuclear industry, which uses it in reactor cores. She moves between bulk and nano constantly, since graphite is simply graphene stacked up; she is proudest of her family tree of carbon, which relates all carbon nanostructures to graphene as the parent.
episodes.image_alt: Irene Suarez-Martinez on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 72: Family Tree of Carbon — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Family Tree of Carbon
episodes.summary: Irene Suarez-Martinez is a materials scientist specialising in carbon, having worked on almost every known carbon material: graphite, diamond, carbon nanoforms and amorphous carbon. She mainly builds atomistic models predicting how these materials behave under different circumstances, and in recent years has added ultra-high temperature experiments.
episodes.image_alt: Irene Suarez-Martinez on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 71: Family Tree of Carbon — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Non-destructive Characterization of Nanomaterials
episodes.summary: Jessica Boland started out studying physics and discovered she enjoyed experiments, including a year in industry at Hewlett Packard learning how to make reflective liquid crystal displays. Her research carries out non-destructive optoelectronic characterisation of nanomaterials, which is vital for developing nanoscale terahertz devices; she is proudest of a terahertz modulator project showing that III-V semiconductor nanowires can modulate terahertz transmission.
episodes.image_alt: Jessica Boland on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 70: Non-destructive Characterization of Nanomaterials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Non-destructive Characterization of Nanomaterials
episodes.summary: Jessica Boland uses terahertz radiation to look at nanomaterials, which are promising candidates for future devices. The episode covers what terahertz radiation is, along with semiconductor nanowires and topological materials.
episodes.image_alt: Jessica Boland on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 69: Non-destructive Characterization of Nanomaterials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanotaxies for Fighting Cancer
episodes.summary: Sean Allen did three rotations in the first year of his PhD, trying a chemistry lab, a dry computational lab and a nanoparticle lab, and the last one simply clicked. His PhD covered self-assembled nanoparticles made from amphiphilic diblock copolymers for immunomodulation, and his postdoc uses lipid-enveloped mesoporous silica nanoparticles for cancer drug delivery; he is conscious that plenty of research makes neat novel nanoparticles, and wants his to actually help.
episodes.image_alt: Sean Allen on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 68: Nanotaxies for Fighting Cancer — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanotaxies for Fighting Cancer
episodes.summary: Sean Allen uses nanoparticles to fight cancer by activating the immune system to do the fighting for you. In his case that means loading nanoparticles with small molecule drugs and delivering them to tumours, where the drugs stop the tumour from switching off the immune cells.
episodes.image_alt: Sean Allen on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 67: Nanotaxies for Fighting Cancer — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Sending Boron Nitride Nanotubes to Space
episodes.affiliation: The University of North Carolina at Greensboro
episodes.summary: Haley Harrison discovered as an undergraduate that she liked working with spectroscopy, learned it was a fundamental tool for nanoscientists, and ran with it. A nanoscientist by training, her research grows out of the fundamental questions that have held back boron nitride nanotube applications; she is proudest of her work on aerogels, extremely effective insulators thanks to their nanoscale pore system.
episodes.image_alt: Haley Harrison on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 66: Sending Boron Nitride Nanotubes to Space — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Sending Boron Nitride Nanotubes to Space
episodes.affiliation: The University of North Carolina at Greensboro
episodes.summary: Haley Harrison works with boron nitride nanotubes, aiming to improve how well boron nitride works alongside high-temperature-stable structural materials. Her work splits in two: improving the stability of boron nitride in solution through surface modification, and finding how to use these materials effectively in structural materials.
episodes.image_alt: Haley Harrison on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 65: Sending Boron Nitride Nanotubes to Space — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Photons on a Chip
episodes.summary: Benjamin Eggleton was fascinated by light from a young age but came at it first through astronomy, doing an honours project on fibre optics in telescopes before, as he puts it, seeing the light and shifting to a PhD on fibre optics. His chips use nanoscale structures etched onto planar substrates with clean-room lithography, controlled to nanometre dimensions; his group's discovery that light and sound waves could be made to interact on these chips was a breakthrough for the field.
episodes.image_alt: Benjamin Eggleton on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 64: Photons on a Chip — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Photons on a Chip
episodes.summary: Benjamin Eggleton works in photonics, the generation, transmission and detection of photons. His focus is photonic chips, thumbnail-sized integrated circuits that dramatically cut the size, weight and power consumption of photonic components, built using nanotechnology and applied in optical communications, sensing and quantum technology.
episodes.image_alt: Benjamin Eggleton on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 63: Photons on a Chip — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Squishy Nanomaterials, their Interactions with Surfaces
episodes.summary: Patrick Spicer learned about science from a group of oceanography researchers, was taught chemical engineering by both academics and industrialists, worked in consumer product development and manufacturing, and then returned to the university. His work has always centred on the flow and structure of soft and squishy materials, liquids that behave as solids or liquids depending on minor changes; he helped develop materials mimicking newborn skin, used in one of the first products protecting premature infants.
episodes.image_alt: Patrick Spicer on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 62: Squishy Nanomaterials, their Interactions with Surfaces — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Cutting Through the Hype about 3D Printing
episodes.summary: Candice Majewski came to the field completely by accident, via a guest lecture on 3D printing, then called rapid prototyping, in the final year of her mechanical engineering degree at Loughborough. Her team explores how materials behave in 3D printing processes and how the resulting parts hold up over time, because it is never as simple as putting a material in the machine and hoping; she singles out work introducing anti-bacterial properties into 3D printed parts.
episodes.image_alt: Candice Majewski on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 60: Cutting Through the Hype about 3D Printing — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Cutting Through the Hype about 3D Printing
episodes.summary: Candice Majewski researches additive manufacturing, better known as 3D printing, a family of processes particularly good at making complex shapes and so opening up designs that used to be hopelessly inefficient to produce. Her specific focus is understanding how materials and processes interact, and using that to develop better and more useful materials.
episodes.image_alt: Candice Majewski on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 59: Cutting Through the Hype about 3D Printing — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Wonderful World of Smart Materials
episodes.summary: Chris Bowen liked chemistry at school but did not want to specialise and was, by his own account, terrible at titration, so materials science appealed to him as a generalist. Ferroelectric ceramics consist of domains with a switchable polarisation direction and show real nanoscale effects; he recently completed a European Research Council Advanced Investigator Award on energy harvesting, converting mechanical vibration using his materials.
episodes.image_alt: Chris Bowen on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 58: Wonderful World of Smart Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Wonderful World of Smart Materials
episodes.summary: Chris Bowen works on functional materials, in particular ferroelectrics, which have fascinating piezoelectric and pyroelectric properties. That makes them useful in pressure and thermal sensors, actuators, SONAR and other transducers, and with UK lockdown ruling out lab work the episode is an introduction to the materials themselves.
episodes.image_alt: Chris Bowen on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 57: Wonderful World of Smart Materials — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: From Nano to the Macro
episodes.summary: Upulie Divisekera's doctoral work looked for new ways to deliver drugs to specific cells, or as she puts it, trying to make clever tiny tablets out of gold. The episode covers her research career, how she ended up in science, and science communication.
episodes.image_alt: Upulie Divisekera on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 55: From Nano to the Macro — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering
episodes.summary: James Armstrong got here accidentally: he trained as a chemist, then took a doctoral training centre PhD at the Bristol Centre for Functional Nanomaterials and ended up doing cartilage tissue engineering. He applies techniques common in nanoscience, such as acoustic trapping and magnetic nanoparticles, to biology; he is proudest of a paper by his student Valeria using sound waves to activate enzymes and assemble fibrinogen gels.
episodes.image_alt: James Armstrong on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 54: Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering
episodes.summary: James Armstrong is a tissue engineer, using cells, materials and chemicals to grow artificial tissues in the lab that could one day replace damaged or diseased tissue. The hard part is recreating the structure of natural tissue, so he has developed a technique that uses sound waves to remotely organise cells into their natural configuration, producing muscle tissue with aligned cells and fibres.
episodes.image_alt: James Armstrong on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 53: Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: From Nano to the Macro
episodes.summary: Upulie Divisekera spent a long time in fundamental cancer research and worked on an immunotherapy, deciding that if she did a PhD it would be in therapies, which led her to nanodelivery mechanisms for anti-cancer agents. She generates particles, primarily from gold nanoparticles, to deliver gene therapies, and is now also thinking about how to treat endometriosis; she is proudest of her work on an anti-CD73 immunotherapy.
episodes.image_alt: Upulie Divisekera on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 56: From Nano to the Macro — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Reading the Fine Print
episodes.affiliation: Centre for Fine Print Research, University of the West of England
episodes.summary: Damien Leech got his job through an off-the-cuff application for a role he thought he had no relevant skills for, applying purely because it sounded fascinating, and discovered his supervisor was a secret physicist too. Print technology demands an understanding of the materials as well as the process, since everything from colour to flow properties is driven at the micro and nanoscale; he recently tracked changing colour tones in the Woodburytype process, which layers translucent films of pigmented gelatin.
episodes.image_alt: Damien Leech on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 52: Reading the Fine Print — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Reading the Fine Print
episodes.affiliation: Centre for Fine Print Research, University of the West of England
episodes.summary: Damien Leech works to resurrect and modernise forgotten 19th century print practices that still hold unique advantages, and to explore wider applications of print technology from 3D printing to screen-printing, in everything from sensor fabrication to artistic use. The episode includes a crash course in 3D printing.
episodes.image_alt: Damien Leech on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 51: Reading the Fine Print — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Fertilizers to Vaccines - Materials Science is Everywhere
episodes.summary: Craig Bunt started out studying pharmacy with a great deal of formulations training, moved into veterinary pharmaceutics research in industry, and has now returned to academia. His research looks mostly at new applications of existing nanotechnologies, early-stage proof-of-concept work; his most controversial success was taste-masking a wildlife control toxic compound.
episodes.image_alt: Craig Bunt on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 50: Fertilizers to Vaccines - Materials Science is Everywhere — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Fertilizers to Vaccines - Materials Science is Everywhere
episodes.summary: Craig Bunt investigates controlled release formulations for uses spanning veterinary and human pharmaceutics and agricultural products. His lab currently focuses on electrospinning nanofibres and 3D printing, applied to wildlife solutions, drug delivery and sustainable controlled release fertilisers.
episodes.image_alt: Craig Bunt on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 49: Fertilizers to Vaccines - Materials Science is Everywhere — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Dancing Electrons Telling Material Stories
episodes.summary: Vivian Tong decided she wanted to be a scientist at the age of six because scientists invented things, and did her PhD using electron backscatter diffraction to study the zirconium alloys used in nuclear reactors. She characterises and manipulates the micro- and nanoscale structure of engineering materials to make them stronger and longer-lasting; in a reactor, the fuel sits inside long, thin-walled zirconium tubes made of small crystals.
episodes.image_alt: Vivian Tong on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 48: Dancing Electrons Telling Material Stories — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Dancing Electrons Telling Material Stories
episodes.summary: Vivian Tong uses electron microscopy to examine the micro-scale crystal structure of materials, specialising in developing electron diffraction techniques. As she puts it, she makes electrons dance in formation by firing them at a material, then interprets photographs of the dancing electrons to tell the life stories of materials used in aeroplanes, drills and computers.
episodes.image_alt: Vivian Tong on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 47: Dancing Electrons Telling Material Stories — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanodrug Deliveries Inspired by Nature
episodes.affiliation: Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI), Germany
episodes.summary: Gregor Fuhrmann finished his PhD at ETH Zurich in 2013 and began working with extracellular vesicles as a postdoc at Imperial College London, developing these natural nanocarriers as drug carriers ever since. His group recently discovered a new class of bacterial vesicles that are low in cytotoxicity yet show inherent antibiotic activity against gram-negative model pathogens.
episodes.image_alt: Gregor Fuhrmann on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 46: Nanodrug Deliveries Inspired by Nature — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Nanodrug Deliveries Inspired by Nature
episodes.affiliation: Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI), Germany
episodes.summary: Gregor Fuhrmann and his group develop biogenic and biomimetic strategies to deliver drugs precisely to their site of action, using nanotechnology to reduce accumulation in other tissue and limit side effects. Biogenic systems such as cell-derived extracellular vesicles come with inherent functionalities and are thought to be less immunogenic than synthetic carriers.
episodes.image_alt: Gregor Fuhrmann on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 45: Nanodrug Deliveries Inspired by Nature — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Using & Abusing Smart Polymers
episodes.summary: Thomas Swift loved his MSc in chemistry and thought he was done with university, until a first job in the R&D arm of a paint manufacturer showed him that more senior managers had a PhD than not, and he took an industrially sponsored doctorate. A polymer chemist by training, he now works on polymers as functional materials, comparing how changes in chemical identity change their real properties and usefulness.
episodes.image_alt: Thomas Swift on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 44: Using & Abusing Smart Polymers — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Using & Abusing Smart Polymers
episodes.summary: Thomas Swift studies functional polymer materials, the large biological and synthetic molecules used to bind and remove things from solutions, and as diagnostic tools, adhesives and property modifiers. We tend to think of plastics as a cheap bulk material, which may be part of why they cause such a global pollution problem, but he argues they are capable of far more.
episodes.image_alt: Thomas Swift on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 43: Using & Abusing Smart Polymers — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Surfaces Made Magical with Nanoparticles
episodes.summary: Tanvir Hussain began his research career with cold spray, a process that accelerates micron-sized particles to supersonic speed so that they stick to a surface without any heating. His field is surface and interface engineering; his group holds a patent on incorporating carbon nanotubes and graphene nanoplatelets into ceramic powders to turn them into functional coatings for tribology.
episodes.image_alt: Dr Tanvir Hussain on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 42: Surfaces Made Magical with Nanoparticles — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Surfaces Made Magical with Nanoparticles
episodes.summary: Tanvir Hussain works on surfaces, interfaces and coatings technologies, with a particular interest in novel materials processing techniques such as thermal spray and cold gas dynamic spray. His latest focus is suspension and solution precursor thermal spraying, making functional coatings from feedstock particles ranging from sub-micron down to the nanometre range.
episodes.image_alt: Dr Tanvir Hussain on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 41: Surfaces Made Magical with Nanoparticles — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Frankenstein on the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Amy Gelmi describes her route as a slippery slope from a PhD in biomaterials and nanoscale characterisation into postdocs that leaned steadily more towards stem cells. One of her primary lines of research uses an atomic force microscope to probe both living cells and the biomaterials they are grown on, letting her watch in real time the changes those cells undergo.
episodes.image_alt: Amy Gelmi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 40: Frankenstein on the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Frankenstein on the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Amy Gelmi studies how stem cells respond to external physical stimuli, using both single-cell and high-throughput approaches, in order to control stem cell fate. The aim is to deliver new platforms for individualised patient tissue engineering, drawing together material chemistry, biology and engineering.
episodes.image_alt: Amy Gelmi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 39: Frankenstein on the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Izzy Jayasinghe trained as a biomedical researcher interested in cellular-level signalling, which happens at nanometre and sub-micron length scales and so drew her towards single molecule imaging and super-resolution microscopy. Much of her work centres on the ryanodine receptor, a giant protein that acts as a key signalling hub in most complex cells and the subject of more than 20,000 published papers.
episodes.image_alt: Izzy Jayasinghe on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 38: Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale
episodes.summary: Izzy Jayasinghe develops and adapts super-resolution optical microscopy methods to visualise proteins, nucleic acids and lipid membranes inside cells. The visual information feeds simulated virtual experiments that show how the interaction of molecules orchestrates life at the nanoscale inside vital organs such as the heart and the brain.
episodes.image_alt: Izzy Jayasinghe on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 37: Visualizing Life at the Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach
episodes.summary: Charlie Wand did a chemistry degree and, between the third and fourth years of an integrated master's, a summer internship at the University of York simulating the self-assembly of block copolymers, which he enjoyed enough to build a career on. He relates chemical structure and composition to bulk material properties through simulation; he is proudest of work at Cambridge developing a new computational approach.
episodes.image_alt: Charlie Wand on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 36: From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach
episodes.summary: Charlie Wand is a computational chemist working at the interface of chemistry and chemical engineering on soft matter, from the liquid crystals in phone displays to the surfactants in shampoo. His simulations represent atoms and molecules as virtual beads in order to investigate material properties, and the episode explains what soft matter actually is and why simulations matter.
episodes.image_alt: Charlie Wand on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 35: From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry
episodes.summary: Laia Castilla i Amoros was in the final year of her bachelor's, wanting to go abroad on an Erasmus exchange, when a couple of nanomaterials courses she had enjoyed pointed her towards her current group. She works on synthesising materials that have not been made at the nanoscale before, and is happiest talking about the first project of her PhD.
episodes.image_alt: Laia Castilla i Amorós on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 34: Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry
episodes.summary: Laia Castilla i Amoros develops the synthesis of multimetallic colloidal nanoparticles. Colloidal chemistry has so far managed only trimetallic nanoparticles, usually containing at least one noble metal; she is pushing towards copper-based, noble-metal-free multimetallic particles for use as catalysts in electrochemical CO2 reduction, where copper is a very promising material.
episodes.image_alt: Laia Castilla i Amorós on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 33: Cooking at Nanoscale with Colloidal Chemistry — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Building New Medicines
episodes.summary: Kameron Kilchrist has typically taken the most interesting path available to him, starting in an undergraduate tissue engineering lab studying composite materials and picking up computational image analysis along the way. His PhD lab built nanoscale drug carriers, so he has thought hard about how nanoparticles self-assemble and disassemble and how they interact with cellular and endosomal membranes; his team recently developed a new assay to measure endosomal disruption in live cells.
episodes.image_alt: Kameron Kilchrist on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 32: Building New Medicines — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Building New Medicines
episodes.summary: Kameron Kilchrist is a biomedical engineer interested in using the latest science at every scale, from proteins and protein complexes through organelles, cells and tissues to the whole organism, to design better drug delivery technologies for the next generation of medicines. The episode covers intracellular drug delivery and what engineering inside a biological system actually involves.
episodes.image_alt: Kameron Kilchrist on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 31: Building New Medicines — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Dancing Light at Nanoscale
episodes.affiliation: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, India
episodes.summary: Siva Shakthi has been fascinated by the world of light since playing with a ball lens as a child and burning paper with focused sunlight. He acknowledges the awkward fit with materials and nanoscience, developing proof-of-concept experiments in microwave photonics; two projects he particularly loves both examined the spectra of a nonlinear process called Brillouin scattering.
episodes.image_alt: Siva Shakthi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 30: Dancing Light at Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Dancing Light at Nanoscale
episodes.affiliation: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, India
episodes.summary: Siva Shakthi works in microwave photonics, exploiting nonlinear optical processes in single-mode optical fibres to build notch filters and optical switches for optical communication and electronic warfare. He is upfront that this is not strictly nanoscience, though the experiments are intended for eventual implementation at the nanoscale; the episode covers how the field of nanophotonics emerged and the role of whispering gallery modes in optics.
episodes.image_alt: Siva Shakthi on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 29: Dancing Light at Nanoscale — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: DNA Origami: Building Synthetic Cells
episodes.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Medical Research, Heidelberg
episodes.summary: Kerstin Göpfrich says simply that she is curious to understand what life actually is and how it could be. She regards living materials as perhaps the most intriguing materials there are, since life works on the basis of nanomachines; her group achieved the division of synthetic cells according to simple physical principles.
episodes.image_alt: Kerstin Göpfrich on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 28: DNA Origami: Building Synthetic Cells — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: DNA Origami: Building Synthetic Cells
episodes.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Medical Research, Heidelberg
episodes.summary: Kerstin Göpfrich asks whether the emergence of life from inanimate building blocks can be replicated in the lab, and whether individual molecules can be assembled into a synthetic cell. Using DNA origami, the nanoscale art of folding DNA, her group designs cellular components and assembles them inside cell-like compartments, so that piece by piece a synthetic cell becomes a reality.
episodes.image_alt: Kerstin Göpfrich on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 27: DNA Origami: Building Synthetic Cells — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Queer and Quantum Magnetism
episodes.summary: Andrew Princep puts his path down largely to serendipity: an undergraduate degree in nanotechnology, a fascination with crystals and crystallography, a summer project with his electromagnetism lecturer, then a masters on neutron scattering and a PhD on X-ray measurements of rare earth intermetallics. As a condensed matter physicist he calls himself a materials scientist with a fundamental bent; he published the most complete measurements of the magnetic properties of yttrium iron garnet.
episodes.image_alt: Andrew Princep on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 26: Queer and Quantum Magnetism — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Queer and Quantum Magnetism
episodes.summary: Andrew Princep uses neutron and X-ray beams to investigate how atoms behave inside materials. A detailed look at how atoms are arranged in a crystal, and at the interactions between them, explains why a material has the properties it does, and should eventually allow materials to be designed with whatever property a specific purpose demands.
episodes.image_alt: Andrew Princep on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 25: Queer and Quantum Magnetism — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Tiny Magnets - What are they for?
episodes.summary: Tim Dreier says he got here by accident, and is only sort of joking: he started graduate school as an organic chemist and changed groups halfway through, ending up applying physical organic chemistry to questions in gold nanocluster chemistry. His research is entirely about making and understanding nanoscale particles, across two complementary fields, soft nanomaterial composites and nanoparticle synthesis.
episodes.image_alt: Tim Dreier on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 24: Tiny Magnets - What are they for? — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Tiny Magnets - What are they for?
episodes.summary: Tim Dreier makes tiny magnets to study how they behave and how we can use them, having previously made polymers containing tiny gold particles and studied how gold forms ultra-tiny particles in solution. The episode is an introduction to magnetism from a self-described novice, and to why nanoscale magnets are worth caring about.
episodes.image_alt: Tim Dreier on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 23: Tiny Magnets - What are they for? — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Tons of Nanomaterials: Big Science and Little Details
episodes.summary: Matthew Jewell joined a superconducting materials research group as an undergraduate at the University of Wisconsin in 1999 and never looked back, going on to the National High Magnetic Field Lab and the ITER fusion project. His research engineers composite superconducting materials at the micro- and nanoscale to make them more robust electrical conductors; at ITER he was part of the team that optimised the 68,000 amp conductor for the magnet system.
episodes.description: Matthew is on the faculty at the University of Wisconsin – Eau Claire, where he investigates the mechanical and electrical properties of superconducting wires, with the goal of making them suitable for large-scale magnet systems such as fusion energy devices and particle accelerators. The work means engineering composite superconducting materials at the micro- and nanoscale to make them more robust electrical conductors. He joined a superconducting materials group as an undergraduate in 1999 and never looked back, via the National High Magnetic Field Lab and a postdoc on the ITER fusion project in France.
episodes.image_alt: Matthew Jewell on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 22: Tons of Nanomaterials: Big Science and Little Details — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Tons of Nanomaterials: Big Science and Little Details
episodes.summary: Matthew Jewell investigates the mechanical and electrical properties of superconducting wires, aiming to make them more suitable for large-scale superconducting magnet systems such as fusion energy devices and particle accelerators. The episode runs from nano to massive, showing how properties at the atomic scale determine the performance of some of the largest scientific machines on the planet.

The work means engineering composite superconducting materials at the micro- and nanoscale to make them more robust electrical conductors. He joined a superconducting materials group as an undergraduate in 1999 and never looked back, via the National High Magnetic Field Lab and a postdoc on the ITER fusion project in France.

episodes.title: Little Lights with Big Ideas
episodes.summary: Rachel Oliver has worked on gallium nitride since her PhD, drawn to it as a good place to explore her overarching interest in the structure-property links of electrical materials. For many materials the nanoscale structure is decisive, and that is particularly true of gallium nitride; she is proudest of her work on atom probe tomography of nitrides.
episodes.description: Rachel is Professor of Materials Science at the University of Cambridge, where she works on gallium nitride — the material the LEDs in energy-efficient light bulbs are actually made of. She looks at the nanoscale structure of the material inside devices like LEDs and engineers it to make them work better, as well as building new nanostructures for new devices. Her overarching interest is the link between a material's structure and its properties, which is what drew her to gallium nitride in the first place.
episodes.image_alt: Rachel Oliver on Under the Microscope podcast, episode 20: Little Lights with Big Ideas — hosted by Dr. Pranoti Kshirsagar, The Science Talk

episodes.title: Little Lights with Big Ideas
episodes.summary: Rachel Oliver works on gallium nitride, the material the LEDs in energy-efficient light bulbs are actually made of. She studies and engineers the nanoscale structure of that material inside devices to make them work better, and builds new nanostructures for new devices; the episode asks why nanostructure matters in an LED and how you go about looking at it.

episodes.title: Graphene Smoothie
episodes.summary: Matthew Diasio went to college intending to study astronomy but was pulled into materials research by a chemistry seminar and some introductory engineering courses, followed by two internships on carbon nanotubes. episodes.title: Playing Snooker with Atoms
episodes.summary: Clara Barker took an undergraduate degree in electronic and electrical engineering and a year's placement at a food packaging machinery company, where asking to work on the machines rather than sit at a desk led her into materials engineering and then a PhD. Her main area is thin film deposition, where changing the gas, pressure, voltage or temperature transforms the result; she once put a thin film onto items used as spinal implants.
episodes.description: Clara is a thin film materials scientist and lab manager at Oxford University, making films often less than a micrometre thick for use as superconductors, solar cells, solid-state batteries and optical coatings on spectacles. Small changes to the gas, pressure, voltage or temperature of the deposition process can transform what a film does, and her high-temperature superconductivity group applies this to changing the temperature at which materials superconduct. She came to materials science from electronic engineering, via a placement improving the barrier properties of food packaging.

episodes.title: Harmonic Generation with a Nanoscale Guitar String
episodes.summary: Michele Celebrano ended up more or less where he started, having coupled ultrashort laser pulses to a scanning near-field optical microscope for his master's thesis in 1990s Milan. He now engineers plasmonic, dielectric and semiconductor antennas and metasurfaces for efficient nonlinear light-by-light conversion at the nanoscale, where photons interact through a material that mediates an otherwise impossible interplay.
episodes.description: Michele is an Associate Professor at Politecnico di Milano, where he engineers plasmonic, dielectric and semiconductor nanoantennas and metasurfaces for nonlinear light-by-light conversion at the nanoscale. A nanoantenna does what a rooftop antenna does — receive and transmit information through electromagnetic waves — except it works with visible and infrared light, which makes it a candidate building block for compact, integrated communication systems. He studies the optical harmonics these structures generate, much as a plucked guitar string sounds different notes.
